title: Ten years without answers: the continuing search for Rochdale’s Jack Stewart
excerpt: Jack Stewart vanished from Spotland on 8 February 2016. His missing-person appeal remains listed a decade later. Here are the original clothing details, what the community did, and how to report information safely.
image_alt: Jack Stewart, missing from Rochdale since 8 February 2016, in the photograph published by Missing People
right_to_reply: Greater Manchester Police and any relatives wishing to contribute verified information or personal memories may contact news@rochdaledaily.co.uk. No participation from the family is requested or presumed.
legal_disclaimer: This story reports an active public charity appeal and historical police/media descriptions, not evidence of death or criminal wrongdoing. Hobbies and family composition have not been independently verified. Potential evidence should be reported directly to police without being disturbed.
body:
Rochdale Daily | Missing persons appeal | 12 October 2026

Ten years after Jack Stewart disappeared from Spotland, a national missing-person charity continues to carry his photograph and an appeal for information. Jack was last reported seen at about 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, at his home on Ings Lane in Rochdale. What happened next remains unknown in the public appeal. For anyone who remembers that morning, or who notices something potentially significant while walking in the area, information can still be passed directly to the police.

Jack's appeal is currently listed by the independent charity Missing People, with reference 16-000774. The charity records him as 68 when he went missing; some original police reporting described him as 69. The important details are the date, location and identifying information, rather than trying to resolve that inconsistency without original records.

Official Missing People appeal: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

THE MORNING JACK WAS LAST SEEN

At around 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, Jack was seen at his home on Ings Lane, Spotland. Police said his disappearance was extremely out of character, noting that he liked routine in his life. That detail matters because those familiar with his everyday movements may be able to distinguish an ordinary journey from a change in habit. The information available publicly does not establish which direction he travelled, what happened after 8am or why he disappeared.

Contemporary reports describe Jack as a white man, approximately 5ft 9in tall, with brown-and-grey hair worn in a distinctive 'teddy boy' style. His clothing was described in early coverage as a BLACK QUILTED JACKET, BLACK JEANS, STRIPED SOCKS and a DARK-COLOURED CHECK SHIRT. These are the last publicly reported clothing details, not proof that any item would remain recognisable today. Colours, fabrics and descriptions may change over time. The police are best placed to assess the significance of any discovery.

Sources: original 2016 Greater Manchester Police appeal, reproduced in subsequent MEN coverage https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/police-new-appeal-over-missing-10871344; later account with clothing description https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; charity appeal https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

HOW ROCHDALE RESPONDED

Local people helped to look for Jack soon after he disappeared. Later reporting records that around 60 members of the public joined a search organised from Brotherod Community Centre, near his home. The response reflected a community unwilling to let a neighbour vanish without notice. Those efforts did not produce a publicly confirmed resolution in the records reviewed for this report.

Source: Manchester Evening News coverage of historic missing Greater Manchester residents https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas

JACK AS A PERSON, NOT JUST A MISSING PERSON

Jack was known to police as someone who valued routine. That is one small glimpse of the life behind the appeal: a man whose ordinary day was sufficiently familiar that his absence immediately stood out. Rochdale Daily has not been able to verify specific hobbies, employment history, or details about a wife, partner, children or surviving relatives from reliable public sources. We will not speculate about them or print supposed family memories without permission.

Anyone close to Jack who wishes to share family-approved memories of his interests, favourite places, the things that made him laugh or his daily routine may contact the newsroom. There is no expectation that relatives should speak publicly. Their privacy and wellbeing come first, and the missing-person appeal does not require the family to relive events for others' curiosity.

TEN YEARS ON: NO CONCLUSIONS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

Jack's continued listing on Missing People means the public appeal has not been withdrawn on the charity's site at the time of this report. It does not establish that he died, that he was harmed by another person, or that the police are pursuing any particular theory. The precise investigative status, searches undertaken since 2016 and any new leads have not been confirmed in a current statement from Greater Manchester Police.

A decade passing does not turn an unverified theory into fact. Whether someone remembers a sighting, has a dated photograph or recalls an unusual circumstance, even a detail that seemed insignificant at the time may be worth submitting to the officers responsible.

IF YOU ARE WALKING YOUR DOG AND FIND SOMETHING CONCERNING

If you come across clothing, personal effects, bones or other material that might be connected to a missing-person case, DO NOT try to decide yourself whether it belongs to Jack. Many items will have entirely unrelated explanations.

If you suspect you have found human remains or a scene requiring an urgent police response, call 999. Do not touch, move, uncover, collect or take anything home; do not dig or disturb the surrounding ground. Keep children and dogs away and avoid walking through the immediate area. Move to a safe position, note the location using a nearby landmark or phone map pin if it is safe to do so, and wait for police instructions.

For a non-urgent recollection, possible sighting or information about the 2016 disappearance, contact Greater Manchester Police on 101 or via https://www.gmp.police.uk. Tell the operator this concerns Jack Stewart, missing from Spotland on 8 February 2016, and provide the Missing People reference 16-000774 as an identifying aid. A charity reference is not necessarily a police incident number.

Please do not post photographs of potentially sensitive evidence, suspected remains, or unverified names online. Do not organise an unsupervised search of private land, woodland or waterways. Any possible discovery should go straight to police, who can preserve and assess evidence and contact families appropriately.

General official guidance on missing-person sightings and reporting: https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person; UK Missing Persons Unit: https://www.nationalcrimeagency.gov.uk/missingpersons

WHAT IF YOU SIMPLY REMEMBER SOMETHING?

People who lived or worked around Ings Lane, Spotland or neighbouring areas in February 2016 might remember a morning journey, conversation or circumstance that they never associated with the disappearance. You do not need to be certain that a memory is significant before discussing it with police. Explain how confident you are, distinguish what you personally saw from what someone else told you, and do not guess to fill gaps.

The charity Missing People also accepts information confidentially. Call or text 116 000, or use the 'Report a sighting' link at https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774. Contacting the charity should not delay a call to police where there is an immediate danger or potential crime scene.

HELP FOR FAMILIES, FRIENDS AND ANYONE AFFECTED

The experience of an unresolved disappearance can affect loved ones and entire communities for years. Missing People offers free, confidential practical and emotional support to relatives, friends and people who are missing themselves. Call or text 116 000. Its family support team can also be reached at family.support@missingpeople.org.uk. Its helpline website lists current operating hours.

Missing People family help: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/help-services/family-support; helpline: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/helpline. If you are distressed by something you have encountered, the police or an appropriate health professional can advise on immediate support; Samaritans offers someone to talk to at any hour on 116 123.

ANY INFORMATION MAY MATTER

Jack Stewart was last seen in Rochdale on 8 February 2016. The clothing described in early appeals — a black quilted jacket, black jeans, striped socks and a dark check shirt — remains a potentially useful historical reference, but identification is the responsibility of trained police and forensic professionals.

For his loved ones, what matters is not speculation but a reliable answer. Ten years later, anyone with real information can still help by passing it to the right people. Rochdale Daily invites Greater Manchester Police and Jack's family, if they wish, to provide any verified updated details for a correction or follow-up; no family member is being asked to take part publicly.

Sources: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774; https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person
